html:
The Upanishads are Sanskrit texts of ancient India, the last layer of the Vedas, which turn from ritual to questions about the self and the ultimate reality. The oldest, such as the Brihadaranyaka and the Chandogya, were composed around the 700s and 600s BCE, late in the Vedic period; a dozen or so "principal" Upanishads date from before the Common Era, and many more were written later.

Growing out of the tradition of the Rigveda, they are often dialogues between teacher and pupil. Their central ideas:

  • Brahman, the one reality behind the world.
  • Atman, the inner self, which is one with Brahman: "you are that".
  • Rebirth and karma, and release from the cycle through knowledge.

These ideas shaped Hinduism and were shared, in changed form, by the Jains and by the Buddha. Adi Shankara built his non-dual Vedanta on commentaries to them. In the 1600s the Mughal prince Dara Shikoh had fifty translated into Persian, and a Latin version of that reached European philosophers. Ram Mohan Roy translated several into English and Bengali, and founded the Brahmo Samaj on their worship of one God.
